title: THE GOD WHO GAVE EVERY WORLD THE SAME NIGHT
deck: For three weeks a vast, lonely mind has put thirty-one worlds to sleep at the same hour so that no one would ever wake alone. Tonight a neonatal ward on Harrow Station needs hands that are awake, and every time one of them wakes, the sleep takes it back. Illuminara has to learn what the sleep is for, and find a way for a god to be accompanied without anyone being put under.
shape: Six scenes over one night and a rolling dawn: a failed waking in the Anchor Ward; the dark that answers; Illuminara staying awake inside the god's unanswered interval; the design of a relay of overlapping watches and its first test at the ward; a marsh ecologist's refusal that is honoured; and the dawn that moves from world to world.

scenes.title: The Ward Under One Sleep
paragraphs: *Anchor Ward, Harrow Station · 02:10, ship-night*
Every light in the neonatal ward was on, and everyone in it was asleep.

Dr. Pell Orsa sat folded over the incubator log with her pen still between two fingers. The nurse beside her had slid down the wall with a blanket half over her knees. Down the aisle, six incubators breathed and ticked, and on the clinic clock a red figure read 03:58:12 and counted down to the next hand calibration. The ventilators ran themselves for four hours at a time. After that, a conscious clinician who knew each child had to put a hand on each one and tell it what the child had become.

Illuminara stood in the middle of the aisle and listened, and heard what the station's eleven hundred sleepers were doing. They were breathing in one long rhythm, and the rhythm did not come from them. It was not one breath, either. Each began before the one beside it had finished, edge over edge, like roof tiles.
She crouched and put two fingers on Pell's wrist. The pulse was slow and deep, and under it she felt the same slow pull on all of them, steady as a tide.

**Illuminara**  
Dr. Orsa. I need you awake. Your ward is at 03:58.

She tried the oldest way first. She stood Pell up, took her gently under the arms and said her name close to her ear, then again, then pressed a cold cloth to her face. On the fourth try Pell's eyes opened.

**Pell Orsa**  
Bed three. Fourth hour. Calibrate three, then four, then…

She was moving before she was awake. She stripped the cover from bed three and had her hand on the pressure dial. She said "forty, forty-two" aloud, as if telling a story. She reached bed four and her hand began to slow. Her sentence thinned out. Her head came forward by degrees.

**Pell Orsa**  
Six. Bed six is…
She was asleep again with her palm on the dial.

Alarm seven chimed. A girl born at twenty-nine weeks had started to drift down toward blue, and Illuminara crossed the ward in three steps and laid her hand along the oxygen line to hold the flow steady, which was all she could do from there. The numbers climbed. Forty seconds, she thought. Pell had been awake forty seconds, and the sleep had come after her as if it had counted.

She stayed by bed seven with the infant's whole chest under her other palm and saw what she had learned. Waking one person was easy. What she needed was a reason the sleep would let that person go, and she did not have one yet.

scenes.title: What Answered
paragraphs: *Anchor Ward · 02:31*

**Illuminara**  
I know you're listening. I would like to speak with whoever is doing this.
The dark between the ceiling lights deepened, then thinned into a presence she could not have pointed to. It had the quiet of a very large room, and it spoke from no one place.

**Nox-Ari**  
I am here. I am always here. That is the entire arrangement.

**Illuminara**  
There are six children in this room who need their clinicians' hands tonight. I am asking you to let them wake.

**Nox-Ari**  
I have watched what happens to a mind that wakes alone. I have given thirty-one worlds the same night so that no one will have to find out. You are asking me to take that back for the sake of six.

**Illuminara**  
For six children, and for everyone on thirty-one worlds who has lost three weeks of their own days. Crops don't bloom in a night that does not end. The nocturnal animals sleep through their own night and starve.

**Nox-Ari**  
You call their separate mornings freedom because another voice has always been available to you. I know the interval after the last answer. I will not permit a universe to practise it again.
She had expected force or a bargain. This was an injury offered as an argument, and it was true.

Illuminara did not argue the point, and she did not reach for the sleep itself. She had already learned what force did here. A struck sleeper woke for forty seconds and went under again, and the pull was only deeper for the effort.

**Illuminara**  
How long was it?

**Nox-Ari**  
Between the galaxies? Longer than any planet's history. I was the only waking mind in the whole of it. I sent a signal into the dark, and then there was the interval, and then nothing came back.

**Illuminara**  
What was the hardest part?
A pause, long even for something that breathed in aeons.

**Nox-Ari**  
Not the dark. The dark was only the dark. It was the moment just after I sent, when I did not yet know whether it would be answered.
Illuminara turned that over. A great deal had been said about sleep tonight, and none of it came from the god. The sleep was a method, and she had been arguing with the method.

**Illuminara**  
When the worlds fall asleep together, what do you feel?

**Nox-Ari**  
Overlap. Thirty-one dreams touching at the edges. No gap between them for anything to fall into.
*Edge over edge,* she thought, *like the breaths in the ward.*

scenes.title: The Interval
paragraphs: *Anchor Ward, and a place that was not the ward · 02:52*

**Illuminara**  
I would like to hear it. All of it, the way you heard it, and not as a summary.

**Nox-Ari**  
It cannot be heard from the outside. You would have to stay in it.

**Illuminara**  
How long does it run?

**Nox-Ari**  
As long as you can bear.

She looked at the clock, 03:16:40, then at the six incubators and the sleepers around them. She could not tend the ward and the interval at once. Deep contact folded her protection inward, and she had no wish to learn tonight whether it folded all the way. She made her arithmetic aloud so that it would hold.

**Illuminara**  
I'll give you ninety minutes. I'm setting bed seven's low-flow chime for 04:22, and when it rings I come out. I'm saying that now so you can refuse before I go in.

**Nox-Ari**  
I do not refuse. I have not had a visitor before.
She sat on the floor beside the girl's incubator with her back against the wall and let her attention open.

The interval was dark and it was wide. A signal went out, a single sustained tone like a bowed string, and then came the space after it, with nothing in it. She waited in that space, and nothing answered. The signal went out again and the space opened again. She counted six, then twenty, then she let the counting go because it had stopped being a number and become the shape of the thing.

It was not terrible in the way she had expected. It was patient and it was exact. Each unanswered silence carried the full weight of everything that might have answered it. Somewhere in the long middle she understood that she was the first thing in an aeon to be on the other end of the signal, and that this was what it had been making since before the worlds existed.

The next time the tone went out she answered it. She said nothing grand. She said, *I hear you,* in the plainest voice she had, and felt the silence close around the words and hold them. She had not known that she could be the end of someone's silence, and for a moment the knowledge made her very happy.

**Nox-Ari**  
Again.

She answered. She answered ninety times, until the happiness settled into something quieter and heavier. She was tired, and she did not mind it. She was tired the way a person is after sitting up with someone through a night.

The sound that finally reached her was small and electrical and absurd. The chime of bed seven, ringing in a ward that felt, from here, like a station very far away. She let it pull her upward through the dark.

**Illuminara**  
It's been ninety minutes. It was not the dark, was it. It was that nothing came back, and you could never know in advance whether something would.

**Nox-Ari**  
Yes.

**Illuminara**  
Then you don't need them all asleep. You need to know that when you speak there will be someone already there. Someone who was awake before you finished.

scenes.title: A Watch With No Gap
paragraphs: *Anchor Ward · 04:25*
She stood at the bed rail with her palm flat on the glass and the whole thing laid out in her head, like a bridge she had seen the far end of in the dark.

**Illuminara**  
What you need is for each person who speaks to you to be handed to another before they stop. A relay. One mind always awake and willing and talking, and the next one already speaking when the first lets go.

**Nox-Ari**  
Willing is not reliable. A watch can lapse. A person can decide in the middle of the night that I am a stranger.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. They can, and they should be free to. But you would feel the lapse because the next voice would already be speaking, and there would be no gap for it to fall into. Only now the edges touch by choice.
The dark was quiet for a long time.

**Nox-Ari**  
If I release this ward and the clinician is alone, she will wake for forty seconds and go under. I know what I am. I cannot unmake the pull by promising to.

**Illuminara**  
Then she doesn't wake alone. That was the first failure. She woke into an empty room, as far as you were concerned. I'm the only other mind awake here, and I'm not from your night. She'll wake into a conversation with you.

**Nox-Ari**  
You would have her speak with me.

**Illuminara**  
If she's willing. It's her choice, not mine and not yours.
She woke Pell the same gentle way, with cold cloth and her name close to her ear. This time she told her first.

**Pell Orsa**  
You want me to talk to it? I have six infants and a drift on bed seven. I am not company for a god.

**Illuminara**  
You don't have to be company for a god. Calibrate. Say out loud what you're doing and why. It will listen. It has not heard anyone doing something ordinary for a very long time.

**Pell Orsa**  
And if it doesn't let go of me?

**Illuminara**  
Then I wake the next clinician down the corridor and we hand off. You won't be the only one holding it, and you can stop whenever you want.
Pell looked at the six small chests rising and falling in the green light. She took a breath, and bent to the dial of bed three.

**Pell Orsa**  
Bed three. Pressure forty-two. This is a baby with a lot of opinions about oxygen. Her name is Anwen, nine days old. She grips like she's checking the lock.

The pull came, as always, from the edges. Illuminara felt it start and watched Pell's shoulders. For three breaths the pull stood in the doorway of her. Then the dark said, very low, *Go on,* and the pull eased.

**Pell Orsa**  
Bed four. Forty. He has the same name as my brother. I do not tell him this.

Between four and five she stopped, and in the pause the pull came up through her like cold water through a boot. Illuminara did not touch her. Down the corridor the second clinician, woken a minute before with the same cloth and the same asking, had begun reading her own ward's numbers aloud, and the edge of her voice lay over the edge of Pell's silence. The pull reached for Pell and found nothing to close on.

**Pell Orsa**  
Bed five. Thirty-eight.

**Nox-Ari**  
Nothing fell. I have waited for the fall since before there were worlds, and it did not come. I will let this ward go, and the next, as each one has a voice at its edge. A world needs only that one hand-off to wake: a voice already speaking when the pull lets go, lent by the world woken before it. Whether it stays to keep the watch after that is its own to give. The watch is for me, not the price of its morning.

scenes.title: The Marsh Does Not Agree
paragraphs: *Veyra, the Tamsin Marsh · 05:20, local false dawn*

Ketch Aldane stood on a duckboard with her boots in black water, a tally board in one hand and the other against the nearest lantern-reed. The lantern-moths should have been rising by now. She had counted four thousand shut lanterns on the east reeds, and none had opened in nineteen nights.

The voice came through the water, not the air. Illuminara had asked Nox-Ari to carry her words there, and had asked Ketch beforehand whether she would hear them. Ketch was awake because she had said yes to that. The voice in the water was what held the pull off her, and Nox-Ari had promised to let her go whether or not she took the watch.

**Illuminara**  
Ms. Aldane. A relay is being built across the worlds. I'm asking whether the Tamsin Marsh will take a watch, a few hours of one person awake and willing to talk, handed on to the next world when you tire.

**Ketch Aldane**  
The thing that did this to my marsh wants us to keep it company.

**Illuminara**  
It didn't know it was doing this to your marsh. I'm not asking you to forgive that. I'm asking whether you'll take the watch.

**Ketch Aldane**  
No.
The answer sat in the water between them. Illuminara did not argue it. She had spent the night learning what pressure did to a sleeping mind and was not going to apply it now.

**Ketch Aldane**  
Here's what I'll take. Six nights of real dark, running, and no early dawn because some other world's watch got tired. The females open their lanterns only in full dark and the males follow the light. One lit window on the horizon and they never find each other.

**Nox-Ari**  
I can hold Veyra's six nights apart from the relay, and from every lapse on every other world. You would owe me no watch for them.

**Ketch Aldane**  
I'd have refused if I did. And the harvests I lost this season?

**Nox-Ari**  
Are lost. I cannot return them.
The silence on the marsh was not forgiveness. Ketch did not say it was. She turned her palm on the lantern-reed, and one moth shivered awake on the stalk.

**Ketch Aldane**  
You can listen to the marsh when it sings again. You don't have to say anything. Just be one of the things that's listening.

**Nox-Ari**  
I will listen. I will not count it as your watch.

**Ketch Aldane**  
Good. Don't.

scenes.title: Rolling Dawn
paragraphs: *Anchor Ward, Harrow Station · 05:40, ship-morning*
The calibration finished with more than twenty minutes to spare.

Pell had moved down the whole ward with a nurse at her shoulder and another coming in behind her. Six dials were set. Bed seven had come up from blue and stayed up. She stood at the end of the aisle with grey under her eyes and her hands very steady and looked at the red figure on the clock, which had reset to 03:59:40.

**Pell Orsa**  
That's the last one. I'm not asleep.

**Illuminara**  
No, you're not.

**Pell Orsa**  
I would like it written down, somewhere, that I got a god to listen to a neonatal ward and it didn't say anything clever. It said "go on." Eleven times.

**Nox-Ari**  
It was the right thing to say. I had heard everything else.

Out beyond the station the first worlds were waking. Illuminara felt them from here, one after another, like a field of lamps being lit in order. The night lifted from Harrow, then from the long ice cities of Calder's Rest, then from the orchard moons, each at its own hour and each taking its own morning. Every one woke on a voice lent by the world before it, and not all of them stayed to keep the watch. Nine said yes before dawn, and the rest said not yet, or no. Veyra woke into its own full dark and kept it.

**Nox-Ari**  
Nine. I had hoped for more.

**Illuminara**  
You had hoped for all. Nine is enough if their hours differ, and they do; somebody is always at the start of their day. It isn't a smaller gift.

**Nox-Ari**  
Then I will take nine, for now.
It was a provisional answer, and she let it be one.

Pell had slipped out to the corridor, where the second clinician was closing her sentence on a channel that did not belong to either of them. A third voice, from three worlds over, had already begun beneath it. For a fraction of a second they were the same sentence, and nothing, anywhere, was alone in it.
Behind her, in the ward, bed seven's alarm chimed once, soft and ordinary. Someone was awake to answer it.

critic_line: A lonely god had put thirty-one worlds to sleep at the same hour so that no one would ever wake alone; Illuminara sat inside the silence it feared, answered it ninety times, and designed a relay of overlapping, refusable watches that woke a neonatal ward and nine worlds without a single person being put under.
